title: Stacking tables with concat

cells.text: merge() joins tables **side by side**. Sometimes you need to stack them **on top of each other** instead, like when you get one file per month with the same columns.

cells.prompt: Press Run to load January–March into jan_mar and April into april. The cell shows april.
cells.code:
import pandas as pd
jan_mar = pd.read_csv("deliveries.csv")
april = pd.read_csv("deliveries_april.csv")
april

cells.text: `pd.concat([jan_mar, april])` stacks the tables, in the order of the list. Notice the square brackets: concat takes a **list** of tables.

cells.prompt: jan_mar has 10 orders and april has 4. What will this print? Pick one, then press Run.
Each table kept its own row labels. What's the label of the last row in the stacked table? Pick one, then press Run.

cells.text: The labels go 0–9 and then start again at 0–3, which is confusing. Add `ignore_index=True` to give fresh labels running from 0 to 13.

cells.prompt: Replace ___ with the setting that makes the row labels run from 0 to 13, then press Run.
hints: ignore + index, joined by an underscore.

cells.text: Store the stacked table in a variable so you can keep working with it, like `all_orders = pd.concat(...)`.

cells.prompt: Your turn: stack the two tables with ignore_index=True and store them in all_orders. Then show the last 5 rows.
hints: Line 1: all_orders = pd.concat([...], ignore_index=True). Line 2: all_orders.tail(5)

cells.prompt: Last one: using all_orders, show the total sales per restaurant, biggest first.
hints: groupby restaurant, pick total, sum, then sort biggest first.

recap: pd.concat([a, b]) stacks tables on top of each other. Add ignore_index=True for fresh row labels.
